pos: n. (Wenceslaus Link, 1483–1547, Augustinian prior, reformer of Altenburg and preacher at Nuremberg)
etymology: Latin Wenceslaus, from Slavic Vaclav, greater glory; German Link, left, left-handed.
biblical_def: Wenceslaus Link was Luther's brother in the Augustinian order before he was his ally in the Reformation. He was prior of the Wittenberg house, then preacher at Nuremberg, then vicar-general of the German Augustinians — the office from which, in 1522, he dissolved the congregation's obligations and released its members to follow their consciences, which is one of the quietest and most consequential acts of the whole period. He married, became pastor at Altenburg, drew up its church order, and ended his life back at Nuremberg preaching in the New Hospital church. He wrote a plain commentary on the Pentateuch for people who owned one book. The thing to notice is the shape of his career: a man in religious orders who used the authority of the order to let men go rather than to hold them. That is the opposite of how ecclesiastical power usually behaves, and it is what the apostle means when he refuses to be a lord over faith. “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vicar-general as an officer who assists a bishop in the exercise of jurisdiction, and dissolve as to break up, to separate a body into its parts.
webster_full: VI'CAR, n. The incumbent of an appropriated or impropriated benefice; a deputy.
DISSOLVE', v. To loosen; to break up; to separate the parts of a body.
PRI'OR, n. The superior of a convent of monks.
CON'VENT, n. An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns.
scriptures: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: The Augustinian vicar-general who used his office to release men rather than bind them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a general suspicion that attaches to all ecclesiastical authority, namely that an office exists to be enlarged. Link's single most important act was to spend his authority downward: as vicar-general he released the German Augustinians from their vows and obligations in 1522, which cost him the thing the office was for.

The principle to recover is that oversight in Scripture is defined by its direction and its temper, not by its reach. Peter sets both in one sentence: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2). Paul's summary of his own ministry is the same thing stated as a negative: “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). He held nothing back and held nobody down.

“be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1) — a vicar-general spending his office downward.

pos: n. (Lazarus Spengler, 1479–1534, town clerk of Nuremberg and lay theologian)
etymology: Latin Lazarus, from Hebrew Eleazar, God hath helped; German Spengler, a tinsmith, a worker in sheet metal.
biblical_def: Lazarus Spengler was the town clerk of Nuremberg and the single most effective layman of the German Reformation. He held no ministerial office and never claimed one; he ran the chancery of a great imperial city and used that position for thirty years to steer Nuremberg into the evangelical settlement and keep it there. He wrote a defence of Luther in 1519 that got him named in the papal bull alongside Luther himself — an unusual distinction for a municipal secretary. He drafted the city's negotiating papers, shaped the Brandenburg-Nuremberg church order of 1533 that became a model across Germany, and corresponded with Luther and Melanchthon as an equal. He also wrote the hymn that puts original sin into German verse so flatly that it was still being sung three centuries later. A city clerk who knows the doctrine and holds the pen in the council chamber can do what no preacher can. “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted” (Pro 11:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clerk as an officer who keeps the records of a court or city, and chancery as a court of equity, also the office where records are kept.
webster_full: CLERK, n. A writer; one who is employed in the business of writing; an officer who keeps the records of a court or city.
CHAN'CERY, n. In Great Britain, the highest court of justice next to parliament; a court of equity.
LA'ITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy.
OR'DINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
scriptures: By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: Nuremberg's town clerk, named in the papal bull with Luther, and author of a hymn on original sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the clerical captivity of theology, the assumption that doctrine is the trade of men in orders and that a layman's part is to receive it. Spengler's career is the standing exception: a municipal officer who argued the case in print, drafted the church order, and wrote a catechetical hymn that taught the doctrine of the fall to more people than most pulpits reached.

The principle to recover is that the word of Christ is to dwell richly in the whole congregation and that the teaching duty attached to it is mutual. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another” (Col 3:16) is addressed to a church, not to a clergy. Spengler's hymn is a layman obeying that verse with a pen, and his city ordinances are the same obedience in another medium: “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted” (Pro 11:11).

“teaching and admonishing one another” (Col 3:16) — a layman named in the papal bull.

pos: n. (Dominicus Schleupner, 1481–1547, preacher at St Sebald in Nuremberg)
etymology: Latin Dominicus, belonging to the Lord; German Schleupner, a Silesian surname.
biblical_def: Dominicus Schleupner came from Silesia to Nuremberg in 1522 as preacher at St Sebald, and with Andreas Osiander at St Lorenz he carried the two great parish pulpits of the city through its change of religion. Nuremberg's Reformation was unusually orderly — no iconoclasm, no rising, no expulsion of the old clergy — and a good part of the reason is that the preaching came first and the ordinances followed it. Schleupner took part in the religious colloquy of March 1525 at which the council heard both sides and then abolished the mass, and he had a hand in the church order that followed. He was the steady one: Osiander had the brilliance and the temper, Schleupner had thirty years in the same pulpit. What a city gets from such a ministry is not an event but a generation of catechised people, which is the only thing that holds when the imperial pressure comes. “Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines colloquy as a conference, mutual discourse of two or more, and parish as the precinct and inhabitants committed to the charge of a minister.
webster_full: COL'LOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a dialogue.
PAR'ISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
OR'DER, n. Regular disposition; a rule or regulation; established mode of proceeding.
EXHORTA'TION, n. The act or practice of exhorting; the act of inciting to laudable deeds.
scriptures: Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
corruption_summary: St Sebald's pulpit, and the orderly Reformation of Nuremberg.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern taste for the dramatic conversion of an institution — the overturned altar, the single decisive council vote — and the corresponding boredom with the thing that actually changes a city, which is a man in the same pulpit for twenty-five years saying the same doctrine in different words.

The principle to recover is Paul's own prescription to a young minister, which is a list of ordinary duties with an extraordinary promise attached. “Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), and then: “continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee” (1Ti 4:16). The word is continue. Nuremberg kept its Reformation through the Interim because its people had been taught, not because its council had voted.

“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — Nuremberg without iconoclasm.
“continue in them” (1Ti 4:16) — the colloquy of March 1525.

pos: n. (Johann Brenz, 1499–1570, reformer of Schwäbisch Hall and of Württemberg)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Brenz, from a south German place-name on the river Brenz.
biblical_def: Johann Brenz heard Luther at the Heidelberg disputation as a student of nineteen and spent the next fifty years working out what he had heard in parishes and duchies. He was preacher at Schwäbisch Hall from 1522, where he wrote a catechism, reformed the schools and the poor relief, and built a model the other Swabian towns copied. When the Interim came he refused and was hunted out of the city, hiding for months in the Württemberg hills. Duke Christoph then made him provost at Stuttgart, and from there he wrote the Württemberg Confession, presented at Trent in 1552, and the great church order of 1559 that governed the duchy for centuries. He was unmovable on one point that cost him Swiss friendships: the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, defended by the doctrine that Christ's human nature shares the attributes of the divine. On that we hold with the Reformed against him, and say so plainly, while owning that few men in that century did more honest parish work. “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ubiquity as existence everywhere at the same time, and provost as the chief magistrate or the head of a collegiate body.
webster_full: UBIQ'UITY, n. Existence in all places or every where at the same time; omnipresence.
PROV'OST, n. A person who is appointed to superintend or preside over something; the chief magistrate of a city.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
scriptures: Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
Act 1:9
And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: The Swabian reformer: a catechism, a confession, a church order, and one doctrine we must refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name here is doctrinal rather than cultural, and it belongs to Brenz himself. To defend a bodily presence of Christ in the Supper he taught that the properties of the divine nature are communicated to the human, so that Christ's body may be everywhere at once. That dissolves the very thing the incarnation asserts. A body that is everywhere is not a body in any sense the Gospels use the word.

The principle to recover is that the ascension was a real departure of a real body to a real place, and Scripture insists on it with a cloud and a promise of return. “And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight” (Act 1:9). Peter then fixes where he now is and for how long: “Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21). We receive Christ at the table by faith, truly, by the Spirit; we do not require his body to be dragged down to the bread.

roots_lines: Greek analambano (G353) — to take up, to receive up; Acts 1:9.
Greek hupolambano (G5274) — to take up, to receive from beneath; Acts 1:9.
Greek apokatastasis (G605) — restitution, restoration to a former state; Acts 3:21.
Greek epimeno (G1961) — to continue, to persevere; 1 Timothy 4:16.
Greek antechomai (G472) — to hold firmly to, to cleave to; Titus 1:9.

“a cloud received him out of their sight” (Act 1:9) — against the ubiquity of Christ's body.
“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — the Württemberg church order, 1559.

pos: n. (Erhard Schnepf, 1495–1558, Lutheran reformer of northern Württemberg)
etymology: German Erhard, from Old High German, honour-hard, strong in honour; Schnepf, a snipe, a woodcock.
biblical_def: Erhard Schnepf was sent into Württemberg in 1534 with Ambrosius Blarer by a duke who had just repossessed his duchy and wanted it evangelical at once. The two men held different doctrines of the Supper, so they split the ground: Schnepf took the north with the Lutheran teaching, Blarer the south with the Swiss, and the pair of them signed the Stuttgart Concord, a one-paragraph formula vague enough to let them work. It is a candid piece of history and worth stating as it stands. Two ministers who could not agree on the sacrament reformed a duchy together by agreeing where they could and dividing the territory where they could not. Schnepf went on to teach at Tübingen and Jena and grew harder with age, ending among the strictest of the Gnesio-Lutherans. The Stuttgart arrangement should be neither celebrated as a model for doctrinal indifference nor despised: it was an emergency measure, taken honestly, by men who told the duke exactly what they disagreed about. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concord as agreement between persons, union in opinion or sentiment, and formulary as a book containing stated and prescribed forms.
webster_full: CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
FORM'ULARY, n. A book containing stated and prescribed forms, as of oaths, declarations or prayers.
DU'CHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke.
ARTICLE, n. A particular part or item of a writing, agreement or creed.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The north half of Württemberg, and a concord written by two men who disagreed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the use of the Stuttgart Concord as a precedent for deliberate vagueness: write the article so that both parties can sign it and let the difference be absorbed by time. That is not what happened in 1534 and the distinction matters. Schnepf and Blarer stated their disagreement to the duke, divided the territory by it, and signed a minimal formula as a working arrangement for a reformation that could not wait. Nobody pretended the question was settled.

The principle to recover is that unity in Scripture is a unity of confession and not a managed silence. “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) is the standard, and nothing short of it should be called agreement. Where that cannot yet be had, an honest division of labour under a stated difference is better than a formula designed to conceal one: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

pos: n. (Hieronymus Baumgartner, 1498–1565, Nuremberg councillor and patron of the Reformation)
etymology: Greek Hieronymos, of a sacred name; German Baumgartner, an orchard-keeper, from Baumgarten, a tree-garden.
biblical_def: Hieronymus Baumgartner studied at Wittenberg under Melanchthon, came home to Nuremberg, entered the council, and spent forty years as one of the men who made that city's decisions. He led the visitation that reorganised the Nuremberg churches, was instrumental in founding the city's high school, negotiated for Nuremberg at the diets, and was captured and held for ransom by a robber-knight in 1544, which the city paid. He is a second example, alongside Spengler, of the particular contribution Nuremberg made: a lay magistracy that was theologically literate because its members had sat in Wittenberg lecture halls, and that therefore did not need to be managed by its clergy or to manage them. The relation between the council and the ministers in that city was better than in most, and the reason is that the councillors knew what the ministers were talking about. “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines visitation as the act of visiting for inspection, and councillor as a member of a council, one who gives advice.
webster_full: VISITA'TION, n. The act of visiting for the purpose of inspecting the state of a church or diocese.
COUN'SELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; a member of a council.
PA'TRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects.
RAN'SOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Pro 24:6
For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
corruption_summary: A Wittenberg-trained councillor, and why Nuremberg's magistrates and ministers got on.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the long quarrel between pulpit and council that marks so many Reformation cities and is usually described as a struggle over jurisdiction. Underneath it is often something simpler: magistrates who did not understand the theology and ministers who did not understand the civic accounts, each suspecting the other of encroachment. Nuremberg was spared the worst of it because men like Baumgartner had read the books.

The principle to recover is that Scripture praises the multiplying of informed counsel and names its absence as a cause of ruin. “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). The emphasis falls on counsel that is actually worth having, which is why the parallel proverb ties it to war, the matter where incompetence is fatal: “For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war” (Pro 24:6).

“Without counsel purposes are disappointed” (Pro 15:22) — the church visitation.
“knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17) — a magistrate trained at Wittenberg.

pos: n. (Andreas Althamer, c. 1500–1539, catechist of Brandenburg-Ansbach)
etymology: Greek Andreas, manly, from aner, a man; German Althamer, from the place-name Althaim, old homestead.
biblical_def: Andreas Althamer wrote the catechism that taught the margraviate of Brandenburg-Ansbach. He was a humanist by training, came into the evangelical movement early, preached at Schwäbisch Gmünd and was driven out, and settled at Ansbach in 1528 under a margrave who wanted his lands reformed. There he produced the Ansbach catechism of 1528 and, with Johann Rurer, the church order that went with it, and he wrote a book on the apparent contradictions of Scripture — a collection of the places where the Bible is said to disagree with itself, each one examined and answered. That second work tells you what he thought the real battle was. A people cannot be catechised out of a book they have been taught to distrust, and the objections circulating among the half-educated of his day are substantially the ones circulating now. He answered them patiently, in order, in print. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, and harmony as the just adaptation of parts to each other.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
HAR'MONY, n. The just adaptation of parts to each other; in theology, the concord of the sacred writers.
MAR'GRAVE, n. Originally, a lord or keeper of the marches or borders; a title of nobility in Germany.
OBJEC'TION, n. That which is presented in opposition; adverse reason or argument.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: The Ansbach catechism, and a book answering the places where Scripture is said to contradict itself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the handling of apparent contradictions in Scripture as a reason for suspicion rather than a call to closer reading. Althamer's method was the right one and is still available: take the objection seriously, state it in its strongest form, go to the text, and show what the objector missed. He did not appeal to mystery and he did not pretend the difficulties were invented.

The principle to recover is that the sufficiency of Scripture is a claim about its adequacy to furnish a man completely, and a claim of that size invites examination. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16), and the purpose clause follows: “That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works” (2Ti 3:17). A catechism is that furnishing begun in childhood.

Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance; Psalm 119:130.

“throughly furnished unto all good works” (2Ti 3:17) — the Ansbach catechism, 1528.
“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — catechising a margraviate.

pos: n. (Johann Eberlin von Günzburg, c. 1470–1533, Franciscan turned evangelical pamphleteer)
etymology: German Johann, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Eberlin, a diminutive of Eber, a wild boar.
biblical_def: Johann Eberlin von Günzburg was a Franciscan preacher of real popularity who read Luther, left the order, and became the most readable pamphleteer of the early German Reformation. His Fifteen Confederates of 1521 is a set of short tracts in the voice of fifteen plain men, each with a complaint and a proposal, ranging from the abuses of the friars to the reform of schools, poor relief, marriage law and the drinking of the nobility. It sold enormously. Eberlin wrote the way people talked, which almost nobody in that century did on purpose, and he aimed every page at a man who could read a little and had an hour. He later became a pastor in Wertheim and in Thuringia and his life ended quietly. He is worth recovering because he answers a question the Reformation is often asked: how did the doctrine get out of the university and into the market square? Partly by men like this, who could put a serious argument in a form a carter would finish. “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pamphlet as a small book consisting of a sheet or sheets stitched but not bound, and tract as a small treatise or book.
webster_full: PAM'PHLET, n. A small book consisting of a sheet of paper, or of sheets stitched together but not bound.
TRACT, n. A treatise or dissertation; but generally, a small treatise or book.
FRI'AR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; a brother of a religious order.
VER'NACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth, as the vernacular tongue.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: The Franciscan who left the order and wrote the Reformation into the market square.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the respectable contempt for popular writing, which treats plainness as a dilution of the argument rather than a cost paid by the writer. Eberlin's pamphlets are not simplified theology; they are serious proposals about schools, poor relief and the marriage law, written by a man who had decided that an argument nobody finishes is an argument nobody made.

The principle to recover is Paul's, and he is blunt about the alternative. “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). He then puts a number on the exchange rate between clarity and display: “I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19). The ratio is two thousand to one and the apostle thinks it is obvious.

pos: n. (Urbanus Rhegius, 1489–1541, reformer of Augsburg and superintendent of Lüneburg)
etymology: Latin urbanus, of the city, courteous; Rhegius, a latinised form of the surname Rieger.
biblical_def: Urbanus Rhegius had one of the most useful gifts of the generation: he could tell the difference between a man who was wrong and a man who was an enemy, and he wrote accordingly. He was preacher at Augsburg through the turbulent 1520s, where the city held Lutherans, Zwinglians and Anabaptists at once and he dealt with all three; then superintendent of Lüneburg from 1530, where he organised the churches of a whole duchy. His best-known book is a manual for preachers on how to handle doctrine before a congregation — what to say plainly, what to leave alone, how to correct an error without destroying the hearer. He wrote a tract on how to speak with the Anabaptists which is notable in that century for assuming that persuasion is the aim. He had been a Roman priest and a humanist and never lost the courtesy of the schools, which in his hands became a pastoral instrument. “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superintendent as one who has the oversight and charge of something, and gainsayer as one who opposes or contradicts.
webster_full: SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
GAINSA'YER, n. One who contradicts or denies what is alleged; an opposer.
CON'VINCE, v. To persuade or satisfy the mind by evidence; to subdue the opposition of the mind.
COUR'TESY, n. Elegance or politeness of manners; civility; complaisance.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: The Augsburg preacher who wrote a manual on correcting a man without destroying him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the collapsing of two different duties into one tone. Error must be named and refuted, and Scripture gives no room for a ministry that will not do it. But the man in front of the minister is not the error, and Rhegius built his whole pastoral method on keeping the distinction. The modern failure usually runs one way — gentleness purchased by never saying what is false — but the opposite failure is just as real and is often mistaken for courage.

The principle to recover is that Paul charges both halves on the same servant in the same breath. “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) requires the refuting. And then: “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth” (2Ti 2:25). The aim named in that verse is the man's repentance, not his defeat.

pos: n. (the Schwabach Articles, 1529, seventeen Lutheran articles drafted as a condition of alliance)
etymology: German Schwabach, a Franconian town; Latin articulus, a joint, a small part, a clause.
biblical_def: The Schwabach Articles are seventeen short statements drawn up in the autumn of 1529, chiefly by Luther, and presented to the south German cities as the price of entering a defensive alliance with Saxony. They cover the Trinity, the person of Christ, original sin, justification by faith alone, the preached word as the means by which the Spirit works, the two sacraments, and the Supper — article ten asserting the true body and blood present in the bread and wine, which was precisely the article Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau could not sign. Those four cities went away and produced the Tetrapolitan Confession instead. The Schwabach Articles then passed into the first part of the Augsburg Confession of the following summer and so into the permanent Lutheran standard. They matter for two reasons. They are the moment the evangelical movement discovered that it could not be a single political body, and they are the moment it decided that a confession, not a treaty, is what defines a church. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alliance as the union of two or more parties by treaty, and creed as a brief authoritative confession of faith.
webster_full: ALLI'ANCE, n. The relation or union between families contracted by marriage; the union between nations by treaty or league.
CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a symbol.
AR'TICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account or system of regulations.
SUBSCRI'BE, v. To attest by writing one's name beneath; to assent to.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Seventeen articles as the price of an alliance, and the parting of the evangelical cities.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the complaint that the Schwabach Articles subordinated the gospel to politics by making doctrine the condition of a military league. The charge inverts what happened. The political men on every side wanted the alliance and wanted the doctrinal question deferred; it was the theologians who insisted that an alliance of churches which did not agree about Christ's presence in the Supper would be an alliance of convenience with a lie at the centre of it.

The principle to recover is that confession precedes confederation, and that a church is constituted by what it says rather than by whom it stands with. The apostolic standard is a common speech, not a common enemy: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10). And the faith is described as a deposit with fixed contents that may be contended for precisely because it has them: “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).
roots_summary: Greek hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, an outline; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly for.
roots_lines: Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern, a form; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to perfectly join together; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly about a thing; Jude 1:3.
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Jude 1:3.
Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation; Isaiah 8:20.

“the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — article ten and the four cities.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — confession before confederation.
